title: From Y to School Hoop
bigQuestion: How did a game from one YMCA gym reach colleges, women's schools and Illinois high schools?

story.title: The Basket Comes Down
story.kicker: In a busy gym in the 1890s, a worn peach basket gives way to an iron hoop.
paragraphs: It is the middle of the 1890s. In a city YMCA gym, a worker climbs a ladder to the balcony rail. An old peach basket hangs there. Its woven sides are cracked from a few winters of hard use.
He pries the basket loose and hands it down. Then he fastens a ring of iron in its place. A net made of cord hangs from the ring. The ring is ten feet above the floor, just like the basket was.

Below him, young men wait with a ball made for the new game. The gym is crowded. Some people stand on the balcony to watch. One day soon, the gym will add a board behind the ring to keep the watchers' hands away.
Across the country, the same change is happening in other gyms. Basketball has left its first room in Springfield. Now it is moving into colleges, women's schools and, soon, public high schools.
story.think: Why would a gym swap a peach basket for an iron ring but keep it at the same height?

lessons.title: Graduates Take the Game
lessons.mainIdea: YMCA teachers trained in Springfield carried basketball to gyms across the United States and to other countries in the 1890s.
reading: The Springfield school trained young men to run YMCA programs. When they finished, they went to work in YMCAs in many cities. They carried Naismith's rules in their bags and in their heads.

The YMCA was a large *network*, or group of connected places. A new idea at one YMCA could reach hundreds of others. Within a few years, basketball was played in YMCA gyms from New England to the West Coast.

YMCA workers also served in other countries. In the 1890s they brought basketball to places such as Canada, China, Japan and France. The game spread through the YMCA before most public schools had gyms.

words.d: a group of connected places or people that share ideas
a person who has finished a course of study at a school

lessons.title: Out of the Y and Into Halls
lessons.mainIdea: As basketball filled YMCA gyms, some teams moved to rented halls, and paid teams began in the late 1890s.
reading: Basketball became so popular that it crowded some YMCA gyms. A few players could take over a room meant for many members. Some YMCA leaders did not like this. Some teams left to play in rented halls and armories.
In 1896 a team in Trenton, New Jersey, charged fans to watch and paid its players. Many histories call it one of the first *professional* games. A professional is someone paid to play.
Some early professional teams played inside a fence of wire or rope called a *cage*. The cage kept the ball from flying into the crowd. For many years, basketball players were nicknamed cagers.

words.d: a person who is paid to play a sport or do a job
a wire or rope fence around some early basketball courts
a large building where soldiers train and keep equipment, sometimes rented for games

lessons.title: Five on a Side
lessons.mainIdea: By 1897 the rules set five players on each team, down from nine in the first game.
reading: Naismith's first game had nine players on each team. He said the number could change with the size of the room. Some early games had even more players, crowded onto small floors.
Too many players made the game rough and hard to follow. Teams began to use fewer players. By 1897 the *rule book* set five players on each side. Five is still the number today.
The change shows how rules grow. The thirteen rules were only a start. Committees at the YMCA, and later at colleges, added and changed rules year by year.

words.d: a printed set of all the rules for a game
a small group chosen to make decisions for a larger group

check.why: A committee is a small group chosen to decide things for a larger group.

check.q: Why did teams begin to use fewer players?
choices: Too many players made the game rough and hard to follow
check.why: Crowded floors made the game rough, so the number of players went down.

lessons.title: A Board Behind the Basket
lessons.mainIdea: Backboards were first added in the 1890s to stop fans on the balcony from reaching the ball.
reading: The first baskets hung from a balcony rail. People stood on that balcony to watch. Some fans reached out and pushed the ball in or knocked it away. The balcony was part of the room, so it became part of the problem.
By the mid-1890s, gyms put a screen or a flat wooden board behind each basket. It was called a *backboard*. Its first job was to block the fans' hands.
Soon the backboard became part of the goal itself. The rules set its size and where it hung. Later backboards were made of glass so fans behind them could still see.

words.d: the flat board behind a basketball hoop
a person who watches a game

lessons.title: Iron Rings and Cord Nets
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1890s, iron rings with cord nets replaced peach baskets, and nets with open bottoms came in the early 1900s.
reading: Peach baskets cracked and broke. They were not built to be hit by a ball all winter. In the 1890s, gyms began to use an iron *hoop*, or ring, with a net of cord hanging from it.
The first nets were closed at the bottom, like the baskets. Some had a chain that someone pulled to drop the ball out. The game still stopped after every goal.
In the early 1900s, nets with open bottoms came into use. The ball could fall straight through. The goal kept its old height of ten feet and its old nickname, the basket.

words.d: the round metal ring that holds the net on a basketball goal
the cord hanging from the hoop

lessons.title: Senda Berenson at Smith College
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 Senda Berenson brought basketball to women students at Smith College in Massachusetts.
reading: *Senda Berenson* was born in 1868 in Lithuania, then part of the Russian Empire. Her family moved to Boston when she was a child. She trained as a physical education teacher.
In 1892 she began teaching at Smith College, a women's college in Northampton, Massachusetts. She read about Naismith's new game. That same year she started teaching it to her students.

On 21 March 1893, Smith students played a game between two classes. Men were not allowed to watch. Many histories call it the first women's college basketball game. In 1985 Berenson was one of the first women named to the Basketball Hall of Fame.

words.d: the teacher who brought basketball to women at Smith College in 1892
a college that admits only women students

lessons.title: A Court in Three Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Berenson wrote women's rules that split the court into three zones, and those rules lasted for decades.
reading: Berenson changed Naismith's rules for her students. Her biggest change split the court into three *zones*. Each player had to stay in her own zone during play.
In the 1890s many doctors and teachers wrongly believed hard exercise was bad for women. Berenson's zones kept the game calmer to answer those worries. Other women's colleges used her rules too.

In 1901 Berenson edited the first official rule guide for women's basketball. Women's rules stayed different from men's for many years. Full-court rules like the men's were not adopted for women's college play until 1971.

words.d: one marked part of the court where a player had to stay
a printed booklet of the official rules

lessons.title: Edwin Henderson in Washington
lessons.mainIdea: In 1904 Edwin Henderson began teaching basketball to Black students in the segregated schools of Washington, D.C.
reading: In the early 1900s, schools in Washington, D.C., were *segregated*. Black and white students had to go to separate schools. Many YMCAs and clubs also kept Black players out.
*Edwin Henderson* was a Black physical education teacher in Washington. In 1904 he took a summer course at Harvard University. He learned basketball there and brought it home to Black students.

Henderson started teams and leagues for Black schools and clubs. He also wrote about Black athletes and fought segregation. In 2013 the Basketball Hall of Fame honored him for opening the game to many players.

words.d: kept apart by race, by law or by custom
a teacher who brought basketball to Black students in Washington, D.C., in 1904

lessons.title: College Teams Play
lessons.mainIdea: Colleges began playing each other in the mid-1890s, including a 1896 game won by the University of Chicago.
reading: On 9 February 1895, the Minnesota State School of Agriculture beat Hamline University 9 to 3. Both schools were in Minnesota. Many histories call it the first basketball game between two colleges.
In January 1896, the University of Chicago played the University of Iowa in Iowa City. Chicago won 15 to 12. Many histories say it was the first college game with five players on each side.

Chicago's *coach* was Amos Alonzo Stagg. He had worked at the Springfield school before he moved to Chicago in 1892. Stagg is better known for football, but he helped bring the new game to a Chicago *campus* too.

words.d: a person who leads and trains a team
the land and buildings of a college or school

lessons.title: Naismith Goes to Kansas
lessons.mainIdea: In 1898 Naismith joined the University of Kansas, and in 1936 he watched basketball become an Olympic sport.
reading: In 1898 the *University of Kansas* hired Naismith. He ran the chapel and taught physical education. He also coached the school's first basketball team, starting that winter.
Naismith coached Kansas until 1907. One of his players, Forrest "Phog" Allen, later coached Kansas for 39 seasons. Naismith lived in Lawrence, Kansas, for the rest of his life and died there in 1939.

In 1936 basketball joined the *Olympic Games* in Berlin, Germany. Coaches raised money so Naismith could go. The games were played outdoors on clay tennis courts. The United States beat Canada 19 to 8 in the final, in the rain.

words.d: the university in Lawrence, Kansas, where Naismith worked from 1898
a world sports meet held every four years

lessons.title: Illinois School Gyms
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first boys basketball state champion in 1908 and its first girls champion in 1977.
reading: The Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*, was founded in 1900. It sets rules for sports between high schools in the state. In 1908 it crowned its first boys basketball *state champion*.

Towns across Illinois built school gyms in the early 1900s. A heated gym let students play all winter. College basketball came to Illinois gyms too. In 1939 the first NCAA men's final was played in Evanston, at Northwestern University's Patten Gym.

Girls had to wait much longer for a state title. Title IX, a federal law passed in 1972, said schools must treat boys and girls fairly. In 1977 the IHSA crowned its first girls basketball state champion.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900
the team that wins the top title in a state
a 1972 U.S. law that bans unfair treatment by sex in schools that get federal money
